final_note: You can explain polymer properties, nanoparticle behaviour and why alloys are stronger than pure metals.

concepts.def: Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in a giant lattice.
A shared pair of electrons between non-metal atoms.
Attraction between metal ions and delocalised electrons.
Small molecules with weak intermolecular forces; low melting points.

walkthroughs.body_html:
A polymer is a long molecule made of repeated monomer units.

Inside a chain: strong covalent bonds.

Between chains: weak intermolecular forces.

Thermoplastics (e.g. poly(ethene)) have no cross-links — chains slide past each other on heating, so they soften and can be remoulded.

Thermosets have covalent cross-links between chains — they keep their shape and char rather than melt.

Nanoparticles are 1–100 nm across — a few hundred atoms each.

As particles shrink, their surface area: volume ratio shoots up. If you cut a cube in half repeatedly, surface area grows fast relative to volume.

Huge surface area means more atoms are exposed, so nanoparticles make excellent catalysts.

Uses: titanium dioxide in sunscreens (blocks UV, looks transparent), silver nanoparticles in antibacterial coatings, catalysts in fuel cells.

Risks: their behaviour in the body and environment is still being studied.

Pure metals are too soft for many jobs — layers slide too easily.

An alloy mixes in atoms of a different size. The bigger or smaller atoms disrupt the layers, so they can't slide as easily → the metal becomes harder.

Examples: steel = iron + carbon. Bronze = copper + tin. Brass = copper + zinc.

Alloys keep many metal properties (shiny, conducting) but with extra strength.

mcqs.q: Why are alloys usually harder than the pure metals they're made from?
options: The extra atoms add covalent bonds
Different-sized atoms disrupt the layers, so they can't slide easily
Alloys have no delocalised electrons
Alloys are ionic, not metallic

mcqs.q: Why do nanoparticles make such good catalysts?
options: They have a very small surface area
They are charged like ions
They have a huge surface area to volume ratio
They melt very easily
Metal atoms themselves move to carry the current.
Metals contain naturally moving protons that act as charge carriers.
Delocalised electrons are free to move through the lattice of positive ions, carrying charge.
Mass is spread evenly throughout the entire atom including the electron shells.

mcqs.q: Where is almost all the mass of an atom located?
options: Electrons contribute significantly to the mass of an atom.
In the nucleus, made up of protons and neutrons.
Isotopes are atoms of different elements with the same mass.
Mass is spread evenly throughout the entire atom including the electron shells.

mcqs.q: What is different between two isotopes of the same element?
options: They have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
Isotopes are atoms of different elements with the same mass.
Mass is spread evenly throughout the entire atom including the electron shells.
Isotopes have different numbers of electrons, which is why their mass differs.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Thermoset”?
options: Polymer that softens on heating and can be reshaped
Mixture of a metal with other elements
Particle 1–100 nm wide — between atoms and bulk
Polymer with cross-links — doesn't melt on heating

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Nanoparticle”?
options: Particle 1–100 nm wide — between atoms and bulk
Ratio that's huge for tiny particles
Long chain made of small repeating units (monomers)
Polymer with cross-links — doesn't melt on heating
